passages.title: Solomon seeks wisdom
passages.summary: Solomon is established as king, and God is with him. He leads the assembly to Gibeon, where the tent of meeting stands. He offers a thousand burnt offerings on the bronze altar. That night God tells him to ask for whatever he wants. Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge to lead the people. God gives him that, with riches and honor besides. Solomon gathers chariots and horsemen. He buys horses from Egypt and makes silver common in Jerusalem.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Why does Solomon ask for wisdom before asking for wealth?

contextNote.title: The opening connects rule with a need for judgment
contextNote.text: Solomon’s request in verse 10 has a purpose attached. He wants wisdom in order to lead and judge a great people. To “go out and come in” is to lead them in daily affairs. Verse 11 lists what he might have asked for and did not. Wealth, honor, long life, and his enemies’ deaths are all named. God adds the first two anyway (verse 12). Verses 14–17 then show the wealth at once, with horses from Egypt.

passages.title: Temple workers and Tyrian cooperation
passages.summary: Solomon decides to build a house for the LORD’s name and a palace. He writes to Huram king of Tyre for cedar and a master craftsman. He admits that even the highest heaven cannot contain God. He offers wheat, barley, wine, and oil for Tyre’s woodcutters. Huram praises the LORD and sends a craftsman of mixed descent. The logs will come by sea to Joppa. Solomon counts the foreigners living in Israel. He makes them carriers, stonecutters, and overseers.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Whose skills and labor make the temple possible?

contextNote.title: A sacred building depends on workers outside the ruling household
contextNote.text: Verse 17 says who did the heavy work on the temple. Solomon counted the foreigners living in the land. Verse 18 assigns them: seventy thousand carriers and eighty thousand stonecutters. The timber and the chief craftsman also come from Tyre (verses 13–16). In verse 6 Solomon says no house can hold God. In 6:32–33 he will pray that God hears foreigners there. People from outside Israel built much of the house where that prayer was offered.

passages.title: The temple building
passages.summary: Solomon begins to build the LORD’s house in Jerusalem. The site is Mount Moriah, at the threshing floor of Ornan. He starts in the fourth year of his reign. The main room is overlaid with fine gold and set with precious stones. The inner room holds two great cherubim whose wings span the width. A veil of blue, purple, and crimson hangs before it. Two tall pillars stand in front of the house. They are named Jachin and Boaz.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: The Seminary manual connects Moriah with sacred space and temple worship. What two names does verse 1 give the site?

contextNote.title: The site connects the new building with an earlier crisis
contextNote.text: Verse 1 gives the temple site two names. One is Ornan’s threshing floor, where a plague stopped (1 Chronicles 21:26–27). The other is Mount Moriah. Genesis 22:2 sends Abraham to “the land of Moriah” to offer Isaac. This is the only verse that calls the temple hill by that name. Both earlier stories end with a death held back. The verse places the altar where those stories were remembered.

passages.title: Temple vessels and bronze work
passages.summary: Solomon makes a bronze altar twenty cubits square. He makes the great basin called the sea, resting on twelve oxen. He makes ten smaller basins and ten gold lampstands. He makes ten tables and a hundred gold bowls. He builds a court for the priests and a great outer court. Huram finishes the pots, shovels, pillars, and stands. The bronze is too much to weigh. The gold altar, tables, lamps, and doors complete the furnishings.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: What different tasks do the temple’s vessels serve?

contextNote.title: Water and metal serve different tasks
contextNote.text: Verse 6 separates two uses of water. The ten basins wash the parts of the burnt offerings. The sea is for the priests to wash in. Exodus 30:18–21 required priests to wash before serving. The tabernacle had one lampstand and one table, and the temple has ten. The text describes the objects by the work they do. Regional metalwork offers comparison without reconstructing these exact vessels.

passages.title: The ark enters the temple
passages.summary: The temple is finished, and Solomon brings in David’s dedicated treasures. The elders gather in Jerusalem at the feast. Levites carry the ark, and the king offers more sacrifices than can be counted. The priests set the ark under the cherubim’s wings. Only the two stone tablets are in it. Singers in fine linen stand with a hundred twenty priests blowing trumpets. They praise the LORD together, for his kindness lasts forever. A cloud fills the house, and the priests cannot stand to serve.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: The Seminary manual compares dedication experiences with later LDS temple worship. What happens when the singers and trumpeters sound “as one” (verse 13)?

contextNote.title: Coordinated sound prepares the scene of shared worship
contextNote.text: Verse 13 stresses unity twice: “as one” and “one sound.” Singers and trumpeters come from different families and duties. Verse 11 says the priests set aside their usual turns for the day. The words they sing are the refrain of Psalm 136. The cloud fills the house at that moment of shared praise. It does not come at the sacrifices in verse 6. Verse 14 says the glory stopped the priests’ work.

passages.title: Solomon’s dedication prayer
passages.summary: Solomon blesses the people and recalls the promise to David. He kneels on a bronze platform and spreads his hands. He says heaven cannot contain God, much less this house. He asks God to hear prayers made toward this place. He names sin, defeat, drought, famine, and sickness. He prays for the foreigner who comes from far away. He prays for Israel in battle and in exile. He asks God to arise and come to his resting place.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: Why does Solomon include foreigners in his prayer?

contextNote.title: The dedication includes people outside the covenant community
contextNote.text: Most of the prayer concerns Israel’s own troubles. Verse 32 turns to a person who is “not of your people.” That person has heard of God’s name and power and has traveled far. Verse 33 asks God to do all the foreigner requests. The aim is that all peoples may know and fear God as Israel does. Solomon has already said that God does not live in the house (verse 18). The house serves prayer, including prayer from outside.

passages.title: Dedication and a conditional promise
passages.summary: When Solomon finishes praying, fire from heaven burns up the offerings. The LORD’s glory fills the house, and the people bow to the ground. The king and people offer thousands of animals. They keep the feast for seven days and the dedication for seven more. The LORD appears to Solomon at night. He promises to hear and heal the land when his people humble themselves and pray. If they turn to other gods, he will uproot them. The house will become a warning to all who pass.

passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: The Seminary manual studies the dedication as an account of divine acceptance. What condition does verse 19 set?

contextNote.title: The promise leaves open the possibility of rejection
contextNote.text: Verse 14 is one of the best-known promises in the book. It is half of a speech. Verse 19 begins the other half with “But if.” The “you” in that verse is plural, so it speaks to the nation. Verse 20 says the house itself can be cast away. Verses 21–22 imagine travelers asking why. The promise and the warning are given together on the same night.

passages.title: Construction, labor, and sea trade
passages.summary: Solomon spends twenty years building the temple and his palace. He rebuilds towns and settles Israelites in them. He fortifies cities for stores, chariots, and horsemen. The remaining Canaanite peoples are made forced laborers. He moves Pharaoh’s daughter out of David’s city. He offers sacrifices on the days and feasts that Moses commanded. He sets the priests, Levites, and gatekeepers in the order David gave. His ships sail with Huram’s sailors and bring gold from Ophir.

passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: How do workers and sailors support Solomon’s kingdom?

contextNote.title: Building achievement requires repeated service afterward
contextNote.text: The building is done, and verse 13 describes what must follow. Offerings are due every day, each Sabbath, each new moon, and at three feasts. The verse says Moses commanded this schedule. Verse 14 adds the priests’ and Levites’ turns that David arranged. Verse 16 then says the house was “completed.” The text counts the work finished when the service is running. A building alone is not the goal.

passages.title: Sheba’s queen and Solomon’s reputation
passages.summary: The queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon with hard questions. He answers all of them. She sees his house, his table, his servants, and his offerings. She says the report did not tell half of his wisdom. She blesses God, who set him on God’s throne to do justice. She gives gold, spices, and precious stones and returns home. Solomon’s gold, ivory throne, and trading ships are described. He rules forty years and dies.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: What does the queen ask about Solomon’s wisdom and God’s care for Israel?

contextNote.title: Admiration describes the court from a visitor's position
contextNote.text: In verse 7 the queen calls Solomon’s servants happy. They hear his wisdom every day. She speaks as a guest who has seen the court at its best. In verse 8 she says God set Solomon on “his throne.” Chronicles thus calls the throne God’s own, where 1 Kings 10:9 says Israel’s. She also names the purpose of a king: justice and righteousness. Chronicles ends Solomon’s story without the failures told in 1 Kings 11.

passages.title: Rehoboam refuses relief
passages.summary: Rehoboam goes to Shechem, where all Israel has come to make him king. Jeroboam and the people ask him to lighten his father’s heavy yoke. He asks for three days. The old men who served Solomon advise kindness. He rejects their advice and asks the young men he grew up with. They tell him to promise a heavier yoke. He answers the people harshly. Israel rejects David’s house, and only Judah’s towns stay with him.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Why does Rehoboam reject the advice to ease the people’s burden?

contextNote.title: Advice differs over how authority is secured
contextNote.text: The elders in verse 7 had served Solomon and seen his rule up close. Their advice has three parts: be kind, please the people, speak good words. The result they promise is lasting loyalty. Verse 8 says Rehoboam rejected this before he heard the other advice. He then asks men of his own age. Their answer treats power as something shown by force (verses 10–11). Verse 15 says God was also at work in the outcome.

passages.title: Defense, migration, and royal families
passages.summary: Rehoboam gathers one hundred eighty thousand soldiers to win back Israel. The prophet Shemaiah brings the LORD’s word against the war. The army listens and goes home. Rehoboam fortifies fifteen cities in Judah and Benjamin. Priests and Levites leave their lands in the north and come to Jerusalem. Jeroboam had removed them and made his own priests. Others who seek the LORD follow them. For three years they strengthen Rehoboam, and his family grows large.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: Why do priests and Levites leave the northern kingdom?

contextNote.title: A prophetic refusal limits the new king's military response
contextNote.text: Rehoboam has an army ready to restore his kingdom. Verse 4 stops it with one message from one prophet. The message calls the northern tribes “your brothers.” It also says, “this thing is of me.” The division is not to be undone by war. The king and the army obey. Verse 17 reports three good years that follow.

passages.title: Shishak and a reduced kingdom
passages.summary: When Rehoboam’s rule is strong, he and all Israel abandon the LORD’s law. In his fifth year Shishak king of Egypt attacks Jerusalem. Shemaiah says they left the LORD, so he has left them to Shishak. The king and the leaders humble themselves and say the LORD is right. The LORD grants some rescue and does not destroy them. Shishak takes the treasures of the temple and palace. Rehoboam replaces Solomon’s gold shields with bronze. He rules seventeen years in all.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: How does Rehoboam respond when Shemaiah explains Judah’s defeat?

contextNote.title: Reduced independence receives an explicit explanation
contextNote.text: The leaders humble themselves in verse 6, and the LORD relents in verse 7. The rescue is partial. Verse 8 says Judah will still serve Shishak. It also gives the reason: they must learn a difference. Serving God is one thing, and serving foreign kingdoms is another. Verses 9–11 show the cost in gold. Bronze shields then keep up the royal show with cheaper metal.

passages.title: Abijah’s speech and war
passages.summary: Abijah king of Judah goes to war against Jeroboam. Judah’s army is half the size of Israel’s. Abijah stands on a hill and speaks to the northern army. He says God gave the kingdom to David’s sons. He says the north has golden calves and has driven out the LORD’s priests. Jeroboam sets an ambush behind Judah. Judah cries to the LORD, and the priests blow the trumpets. God defeats Israel, and Abijah takes Bethel and other towns.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: What reasons does Abijah give for Judah’s trust in God?

contextNote.title: A battle speech argues through the institutions of worship
contextNote.text: Abijah’s speech does not boast of soldiers, since he has fewer. His case rests on worship. Judah has Aaron’s priests, daily offerings, and the lamps (verses 10–11). Verse 12 says God is at Judah’s head, with priests and trumpets. He still calls the enemy “children of Israel.” He calls the LORD the God of their fathers too. Verse 18 gives the writer’s reason for the victory: Judah relied on the LORD.

passages.title: Asa changes worship and asks for help
passages.summary: Asa does what is good and right. He removes foreign altars and tells Judah to seek the LORD. The land has ten years of peace. He builds walled cities and trains a large army. Zerah the Cushite comes against him with a far greater force. Asa prays that the LORD helps the weak as easily as the strong. The LORD strikes the Cushites, and they flee. Judah carries home much plunder, with sheep and camels.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me invites study of Asa’s trust during danger. On whom does Asa say Judah relies (verse 11)?

contextNote.title: Preparation and petition share the account of defense
contextNote.text: Asa has walls, towers, and a trained army (verses 6–8). His prayer in verse 11 does not mention them. He says only the LORD can help, whether the side is strong or weak. He says, “we rely on you.” He also makes the battle God’s: no man should prevail against him. The chapter shows preparation and prayer side by side. Chapter 16 will test whether Asa keeps relying this way.

passages.title: Azariah’s warning and covenant
passages.summary: God’s Spirit comes on Azariah, who meets Asa after the victory. He says the LORD is with them while they are with him. Israel once lived long without a teaching priest or law. Asa takes courage and removes idols from the land. He repairs the LORD’s altar. Many come to him from the northern tribes. The people swear a covenant with shouting and trumpets and great joy. Asa even removes his grandmother from her position for her idol.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies perseverance and trust through Asa’s reforms. What does Asa do after hearing the prophet (verse 8)?

contextNote.title: A spoken warning becomes a public commitment
contextNote.text: Verse 8 says Asa “took courage” when he heard the prophet. Reform takes courage because it reaches into his own house. Verse 16 shows it: he removes his grandmother from her rank. Verse 9 says people from the north joined him. They came when they saw that God was with him. Verse 2 states the rule beneath the whole chapter. The LORD is found by those who seek him.

passages.title: Asa’s alliance and anger
passages.summary: Baasha king of Israel fortifies Ramah to shut Judah in. Asa sends temple and palace treasure to the king of Syria. Syria attacks Israel’s northern towns, and Baasha stops building. The seer Hanani tells Asa he relied on Syria and not on the LORD. He reminds him of the victory over the Cushites. From now on Asa will have wars. Asa puts the seer in prison and mistreats some of the people. Late in life his feet are diseased, and he seeks only physicians.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me compares where Asa places his trust at different times. How does Asa treat the seer in verse 10?

contextNote.title: A ruler's response to criticism changes his judgment
contextNote.text: In 14:11 Asa prayed, “we rely on you.” Hanani uses that same word against him in verses 7–8. The seer’s argument is Asa’s own past. God handled a much larger army when Asa asked. In 15:8 Asa heard a prophet and took courage. In verse 10 he hears one and reaches for the prison. The verse adds that he oppressed some of the people at that time.

passages.title: Jehoshaphat teaches and strengthens Judah
passages.summary: Jehoshaphat becomes king and strengthens Judah against Israel. He follows the ways of David and does not seek the Baals. The LORD establishes his kingdom, and he grows rich. In his third year he sends officials, Levites, and priests through Judah. They carry the book of the LORD’s law and teach in every city. Fear of the LORD falls on the nearby kingdoms. Philistines and Arabs bring him tribute. He builds forts and keeps a large army.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: How does Jehoshaphat use teachers to help his people learn God’s law?

contextNote.title: Instruction carries the law beyond the capital
contextNote.text: Verses 7–8 name the teaching team. It has five officials, nine Levites, and two priests. Verse 9 says they carried the book of the law with them. They went to the people’s towns; the people did not come to them. Royal officers and temple staff taught together. Verse 10 follows with peace on Judah’s borders. The writer sets that peace beside the teaching before he lists the army.

passages.title: Micaiah and the war with Ahab
passages.summary: Jehoshaphat is rich and allied to Ahab by marriage. Ahab asks him to help retake Ramoth Gilead. Four hundred prophets promise victory. Jehoshaphat asks for another, and Micaiah is called. Micaiah sees Israel scattered and describes a lying spirit in the prophets’ mouths. Ahab jails him and goes to battle in disguise. The enemy surrounds Jehoshaphat, and he cries out and is spared. A random arrow strikes Ahab, and he dies at sunset.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Micaiah’s truthful speech under pressure. What does the messenger ask of Micaiah in verse 12?

contextNote.title: Approved predictions place pressure on an independent speaker
contextNote.text: The messenger in verse 12 asks Micaiah to match the others. Four hundred voices already agree, and the kings are waiting. Micaiah answers that he will say what God says (verse 13). Jehoshaphat is the one who asked for a true word (verses 4 and 6). He hears it and still rides into battle (verse 28). Verse 31 says the LORD helped him when he cried out. Chapter 19:2 rebukes him for the alliance.

passages.title: Correction and impartial judgment
passages.summary: Jehoshaphat returns safely, and the seer Jehu rebukes him for helping the wicked. Yet some good is found in him. The king travels among the people and brings them back to the LORD. He appoints judges in every fortified city. He tells them they judge for the LORD, not for man. In Jerusalem he sets up a court of Levites, priests, and family heads. The chief priest leads in the LORD’s matters. A leader of Judah handles the king’s matters.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: The Seminary manual connects correction with faithful service. What three things does verse 7 say are not found with the LORD?

contextNote.title: Judicial work requires limits on personal advantage
contextNote.text: Jehoshaphat accepts a seer’s rebuke in verses 2–3. His father had jailed that seer’s father (16:10). His response is to reform the courts. Verse 6 tells the judges whose work they do. Verse 7 sets their standard by God’s character. With him there is no injustice, no favoritism, and no bribe. Verse 11 divides religious cases from royal ones under two chiefs.

passages.title: Prayer, Jahaziel, and deliverance
passages.summary: A great army from Moab, Ammon, and Mount Seir comes against Judah. Jehoshaphat is afraid and calls a fast. All Judah gathers with wives and children. The king prays and admits they have no strength and no plan. The Spirit comes on Jahaziel, a Levite, who says the battle is God’s. Next morning singers march ahead of the army giving thanks. The enemy armies turn on one another. Judah gathers plunder for three days and blesses the LORD.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies prayer, trust, and prophetic encouragement. What does the king admit in verse 12?

contextNote.title: Public prayer names the limits of royal knowledge
contextNote.text: A king is expected to have a plan. In verse 12 Jehoshaphat says in public that he has none. He says, “We don’t know what to do.” Verse 13 notes who is listening: whole families with little ones. The answer comes through a Levite of a singers’ family (verse 14). He says they will not need to fight (verse 17). In verse 21 the king puts a choir ahead of the soldiers.

passages.title: Jehoram’s violence and decline
passages.summary: Jehoshaphat gives his sons gifts and cities and leaves the kingdom to Jehoram. Jehoram kills all his brothers and some of the princes. He marries Ahab’s daughter and follows Israel’s kings. The LORD spares David’s house because of the covenant. Edom and Libnah revolt. A letter from Elijah says Jehoram will die of disease. Raiders carry off his goods, wives, and sons. He dies in great pain, and no one regrets his death.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: How do Jehoram’s choices affect his brothers and the people he rules?

contextNote.title: Securing a throne can destroy the household that supports it
contextNote.text: Verse 3 says the father provided for every son. Jehoram sees his brothers as rivals and kills them (verse 4). The rest of the chapter returns the loss to him. Subject peoples break away (verses 8–10). Raiders take his own sons, all but the youngest (verse 17). Elijah’s letter calls the murdered brothers better men than he (verse 13). Verse 20 says he departed “with no one’s regret.”

passages.title: Ahaziah dies and Joash is hidden
passages.summary: Ahaziah becomes king of Judah. His mother Athaliah advises him to do evil. He joins Israel’s king in war and visits him at Jezreel. Jehu, who is destroying Ahab’s house, kills Ahaziah too. Athaliah then kills the royal children of Judah. Jehoshabeath, the king’s daughter, steals away the baby Joash. She hides him and his nurse in a bedroom. He stays hidden in God’s house for six years while Athaliah rules.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: What do Jehoshabeath and the nurse risk by hiding Joash?

contextNote.title: Protection makes a later coronation possible
contextNote.text: Two women shape this chapter. Verse 3 says Athaliah counseled her son to do wrong. Verse 10 says she killed her own grandchildren for the throne. Verse 11 names the woman who stopped her. Jehoshabeath was a king’s daughter and the wife of the priest Jehoiada. That marriage explains how a child could be hidden in the temple. For six years the line of David depends on her secret.

passages.title: Jehoiada installs Joash
passages.summary: In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada makes a pact with the guard captains. They gather Levites and family heads from all Judah. Guards surround the young king with weapons from the temple. They crown Joash, hand him the testimony, and shout. Athaliah cries treason and is put to death outside the temple. Jehoiada makes a covenant with the people and the king. They tear down Baal’s temple. Gatekeepers are posted, and the city is quiet.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: Why does Jehoiada ask the people to promise loyalty to God when Joash becomes king?

contextNote.title: A coronation restores obligations as well as a ruler
contextNote.text: The crowning in verse 11 includes “the testimony.” Deuteronomy 17:18–19 required a king to keep a copy of the law. Verse 16 then binds three parties: priest, people, and king. Its aim is that they should be the LORD’s people. A seven-year-old king is one party among others. The covenant puts duties on the throne, not only a boy. Verses 18–19 restore the temple order that David set.

passages.title: Temple repair and Zechariah’s death
passages.summary: Joash does right all the days of the priest Jehoiada. He collects money in a chest and repairs the temple. Jehoiada dies very old and is buried among the kings. Then Judah’s princes persuade the king to leave the LORD’s house. Prophets warn them, and they do not listen. The Spirit comes on Zechariah, Jehoiada’s son, who rebukes the people. At the king’s command they stone him in the temple court. A small Syrian army defeats Judah, and Joash’s servants kill him.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: Why does Joash reject correction after Jehoiada’s death?

contextNote.title: The king forgets the care that preserved his position
contextNote.text: Jehoiada and his wife saved Joash’s life as a baby (22:11). They hid him in the temple for six years. Verse 22 says the king did not remember that kindness. He has their son killed in the court of that same house (verse 21). Zechariah’s last words ask the LORD to see and repay. The burials tell the verdict. The priest lies among the kings (verse 16), and the king does not (verse 25).

passages.title: Amaziah’s victories and defeat
passages.summary: Amaziah does right, but not with a whole heart. He hires a hundred thousand soldiers from Israel. A man of God says to send them home, and he obeys at a loss. He defeats Edom and then worships Edom’s gods. A prophet asks why he seeks gods that could not save their own people. The king threatens him into silence. Amaziah challenges Israel’s king and is badly beaten. Jerusalem’s wall is broken, and he later dies by conspiracy.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: How does Amaziah respond differently to his two warnings?

contextNote.title: A successful king tries to silence the judgment of success
contextNote.text: The first warning cost Amaziah a hundred talents of silver (verses 6–9). He asked about the money and still obeyed (verse 10). The second warning comes after a victory. The prophet’s logic in verse 15 is simple: these gods lost. In verse 16 the king cuts him off and hints at violence. He says no one appointed the prophet as a royal adviser. Success has changed how he hears correction.

passages.title: Uzziah’s strength and forbidden incense
passages.summary: Uzziah becomes king at sixteen and rules fifty-two years. He seeks God, and God gives him success. He defeats the Philistines, builds towers, digs cisterns, and loves farming. His army is large and has new war machines. When he is strong, his heart grows proud. He enters the temple to burn incense on the altar. Eighty priests confront him, and he becomes angry. A skin disease breaks out on his forehead, and he lives apart until he dies.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies humility and the limits on Uzziah’s incense offering. What do the priests tell the king in verse 18?

contextNote.title: Royal success does not confer every sacred role
contextNote.text: Verse 16 dates the fall: “when he was strong.” Uzziah has succeeded at war, building, and farming. He now reaches for a task that is not a king’s. Numbers 18:7 gives the incense altar to Aaron’s sons alone. In verse 18 eighty-one priests tell the king to leave. Verse 17 calls them men of courage. Verse 19 says the disease appeared while he was raging at them.

passages.title: Jotham builds and governs
passages.summary: Jotham becomes king at twenty-five and rules sixteen years. He does what is right, as his father Uzziah did. Unlike his father he does not enter the LORD’s temple. The people still act corruptly. He builds the upper gate of the temple and much on the city wall. He builds towns in the hills and forts in the forests. He defeats Ammon, which pays him tribute. He grows strong because he orders his ways before the LORD.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: What can a faithful leader do when others continue doing wrong?

contextNote.title: A ruler's conduct does not automatically change the people
contextNote.text: Verse 2 makes three statements in a row. Jotham did right. He stayed out of the temple, so he learned from his father’s fall. The people still acted corruptly. A good king, the verse admits, does not make a good people. Verse 6 credits his strength to his own steady conduct. Isaiah 1:1 and Micah 1:1 place those prophets’ warnings in his reign.

passages.title: Ahaz, captives, and Oded’s intervention
passages.summary: Ahaz makes idols and burns his children as offerings. Syria defeats him and takes captives. Israel’s king kills many of Judah’s soldiers and carries off women and children. The prophet Oded meets the army at Samaria. He says they have killed in rage and must not enslave their kin. Four leaders of Ephraim agree and stop the army. They clothe, feed, and carry the captives back to Jericho. Ahaz then seeks Assyria’s help, worships Syria’s gods, and shuts the temple.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: How do the northern leaders turn a victory into care for their captives?

contextNote.title: A prophetic appeal changes the treatment of defeated enemies
contextNote.text: Oded does not deny that the victory came from God (verse 9). He denies that it permits enslaving “your brothers.” Verse 10 asks whether the victors have no sins of their own. Verse 11 then gives the order: send them back. Four named leaders face down the army (verses 12–13). Verse 15 lists their care: clothes, sandals, food, oil, and donkeys for the weak. Jesus’s story in Luke 10:33–35 uses several of the same details.

passages.title: Hezekiah restores temple service
passages.summary: Hezekiah opens the temple doors in the first month of his reign. He tells the priests and Levites to make themselves and the house holy. They carry out the filth and finish in sixteen days. The king and the city leaders bring sin offerings for all Israel. Levites play the instruments David appointed, and the assembly bows. The people bring so many offerings that the priests need help. The Levites assist them. Hezekiah and the people rejoice at how quickly it was done.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: What work must the priests and Levites finish before temple worship can begin again?

contextNote.title: Restoration joins specialized duties with broad participation
contextNote.text: The chapter follows a set order. First the house is cleaned (verses 15–17). Then offerings are made for sin (verses 21–24). Then the music begins (verses 25–30), and the people bring their gifts (verse 31). Verse 34 admits a shortage of ready priests, and Levites fill the gap. Verse 36 gives the reason for the joy. God had prepared the people, and the work was done “suddenly.”

passages.title: Passover invitations and pardon
passages.summary: Hezekiah invites all Israel and Judah to keep the Passover in Jerusalem. It is held in the second month because the priests were not ready. Couriers carry letters north to Ephraim and Manasseh. Many laugh at them, but some humble themselves and come. Many who come have not made themselves clean. They eat anyway, and Hezekiah prays for their pardon. The LORD hears him and heals the people. The feast is so glad that they keep it seven more days.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies welcome, pardon, and peacemaking at Passover. For whom does Hezekiah pray in verses 18–19?

contextNote.title: The invitation reaches beyond perfect ritual preparation
contextNote.text: Verse 18 admits that the rule was broken. Many from the north ate the Passover without being clean. Hezekiah does not send them away. His prayer asks pardon for all who truly seek God (verses 18–19). Verse 20 says the LORD listened. Even the month was moved to make the feast possible (verses 2–3). Numbers 9:10–11 had allowed a second-month Passover for people who were not ready.

passages.title: Offerings and faithful distribution
passages.summary: After the feast the people break down the idols and altars across the land. Hezekiah sets the priests and Levites in their turns of service. He gives from his own herds for the regular offerings. He tells the people to give the priests’ and Levites’ share. They bring grain, wine, oil, and honey in heaps for four months. The chief priest says there is enough and plenty left over. Storerooms are prepared and keepers named. Men are chosen to hand out portions fairly in every town.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

lds.text: How do careful storage and fair sharing support the temple workers’ families?

contextNote.title: Distribution makes continued worship possible for households
contextNote.text: Verse 4 gives the purpose of the gifts. Priests and Levites should be free to give themselves to the LORD’s law. The people respond with heaps (verses 5–7). Verse 10 reports enough to eat and much to spare. Verses 12–15 name the keepers and require fair shares for great and small. Verse 18 extends the list to wives, sons, daughters, and little ones. Worship continues because whole households are fed.

passages.title: Sennacherib’s challenge and Hezekiah’s response
passages.summary: Sennacherib of Assyria invades Judah and camps against its walled cities. Hezekiah stops the springs outside Jerusalem and repairs the wall. He makes weapons and tells the people that a greater one is with them. Assyrian officers shout insults at the people on the wall. Hezekiah and Isaiah cry to heaven. An angel destroys the Assyrian commanders, and Sennacherib goes home in shame. Later Hezekiah is sick, grows proud, and humbles himself. He also brings water down to the west side of David’s city.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The Seminary manual highlights Hezekiah’s humility. What practical steps does Hezekiah take in verses 3–5?

contextNote.title: Defense combines work and trust
contextNote.text: Hezekiah’s first response is practical. He blocks the water an army would need (verses 3–4). Verse 5 lists a repaired wall, towers, a second wall, and weapons. His speech in verses 7–8 then asks the people to trust God. The account sets defense and prayer together. Assyrian records describe the campaign from the attacking king’s side. Chronicles leaves out the tribute reported in 2 Kings 18:14–16.

passages.title: Manasseh’s repentance and Amon’s refusal
passages.summary: Manasseh rules fifty-five years and does great evil. He rebuilds the high places and sets an idol in God’s house. He burns his sons, uses sorcery, and ignores every warning. Assyrian commanders capture him and take him to Babylon in chains. In distress he humbles himself and prays. God hears and brings him back to Jerusalem. He removes the idols and repairs the LORD’s altar. His son Amon does evil, does not humble himself, and is killed.

contextNote.title: This account gives Manasseh a change absent from Kings
contextNote.text: Second Kings 21 tells of Manasseh’s sins and nothing more. Chronicles adds a capture, a prayer, and a return (verses 11–13). Verse 12 marks the turn: he was in distress, and he humbled himself. Verse 13 says God was moved and heard him. The worst king in the book is not beyond being heard. His reform is real but incomplete (verse 17). Verse 23 says Amon did not humble himself as his father had.

passages.title: Josiah changes worship and seeks Huldah's answer
passages.summary: Josiah becomes king at eight. At sixteen he begins to seek God, and at twenty he clears away the idols. He carries the reform into the northern lands. In his eighteenth year he repairs the temple with honest workmen. While the money is brought out, the priest Hilkiah finds the book of the law. The king hears it and tears his clothes. His officials consult the prophetess Huldah, who confirms the coming disaster. Josiah gathers the people and renews the covenant.

contextNote.title: A restored building brings a disruptive text to light
contextNote.text: In Chronicles Josiah has been reforming for years before the book appears (verses 3–7). The book is found during ordinary work with the temple money (verse 14). Its words still make him tear his clothes (verse 19). A sincere reformer learns how much he did not know. Verse 22 sends his chief officials to Huldah. She speaks for the LORD and confirms what the book says (verses 23–25). Her answer leads to a public covenant (verses 29–32).

passages.title: Josiah’s Passover and death
passages.summary: Josiah keeps the Passover in Jerusalem on the proper day. He sets the priests and Levites in their places. He and his officials give thousands of animals for the people. No Passover like it had been kept since Samuel’s time. Later Pharaoh Neco marches north to fight at Carchemish. Josiah goes out against him. Neco says God sent him and warns Josiah to turn back. Josiah fights in disguise, is shot by archers, and dies in Jerusalem.

contextNote.title: A praised ruler still makes a fatal decision
contextNote.text: Verse 20 begins “After all this,” meaning after the temple and the Passover. Josiah’s record gives no protection for the next choice. The warning comes from a foreign king (verse 21). Verse 22 says his words were “from the mouth of God.” Josiah once sent to a prophetess to test a book. Here he does not ask anyone. His disguise recalls Ahab’s in 18:29, and it works no better.

passages.title: Exile and Cyrus’s proclamation
passages.summary: Judah’s last four kings rule under Egypt and then Babylon. Zedekiah will not humble himself before the prophet Jeremiah. He breaks an oath he swore by God to Nebuchadnezzar. The LORD sends messengers again and again, out of pity for his people. They mock the prophets until there is no remedy. The Babylonians kill, burn the temple, and break down Jerusalem’s wall. The survivors become servants in Babylon for seventy years. Then Cyrus king of Persia permits the people to go up and rebuild.

contextNote.title: The last royal speech opens a road beyond exile
contextNote.text: Verses 15–16 explain the exile before verse 23 ends it. God sent messengers out of compassion, and they were mocked. The final speech comes from Cyrus, a foreign ruler. It allows a return and the rebuilding of a temple. The book’s last words are “let him go up.” The Cyrus Cylinder gives wider context for Persian restoration claims. It does not name this return or prove every detail of the speech.

events.title: Solomon seeks wisdom
events.summary: Solomon is established as king, and God is with him. He leads the assembly to Gibeon, where the tent of meeting stands. He offers a thousand burnt offerings on the bronze altar. That night God tells him to ask for whatever he wants. Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge to lead the people. God gives him that, with riches and honor besides. Solomon gathers chariots and horsemen. He buys horses from Egypt and makes silver common in Jerusalem.
events.detail: Solomon’s request in verse 10 has a purpose attached. He wants wisdom in order to lead and judge a great people. To “go out and come in” is to lead them in daily affairs. Verse 11 lists what he might have asked for and did not. Wealth, honor, long life, and his enemies’ deaths are all named. God adds the first two anyway (verse 12). Verses 14–17 then show the wealth at once, with horses from Egypt.

events.title: Temple workers and Tyrian cooperation
events.summary: Solomon decides to build a house for the LORD’s name and a palace. He writes to Huram king of Tyre for cedar and a master craftsman. He admits that even the highest heaven cannot contain God. He offers wheat, barley, wine, and oil for Tyre’s woodcutters. Huram praises the LORD and sends a craftsman of mixed descent. The logs will come by sea to Joppa. Solomon counts the foreigners living in Israel. He makes them carriers, stonecutters, and overseers.
events.detail: Verse 17 says who did the heavy work on the temple. Solomon counted the foreigners living in the land. Verse 18 assigns them: seventy thousand carriers and eighty thousand stonecutters. The timber and the chief craftsman also come from Tyre (verses 13–16). In verse 6 Solomon says no house can hold God. In 6:32–33 he will pray that God hears foreigners there. People from outside Israel built much of the house where that prayer was offered.

events.title: The temple building
events.summary: Solomon begins to build the LORD’s house in Jerusalem. The site is Mount Moriah, at the threshing floor of Ornan. He starts in the fourth year of his reign. The main room is overlaid with fine gold and set with precious stones. The inner room holds two great cherubim whose wings span the width. A veil of blue, purple, and crimson hangs before it. Two tall pillars stand in front of the house. They are named Jachin and Boaz.
events.detail: Verse 1 gives the temple site two names. One is Ornan’s threshing floor, where a plague stopped (1 Chronicles 21:26–27). The other is Mount Moriah. Genesis 22:2 sends Abraham to “the land of Moriah” to offer Isaac. This is the only verse that calls the temple hill by that name. Both earlier stories end with a death held back. The verse places the altar where those stories were remembered.

events.title: Temple vessels and bronze work
events.summary: Solomon makes a bronze altar twenty cubits square. He makes the great basin called the sea, resting on twelve oxen. He makes ten smaller basins and ten gold lampstands. He makes ten tables and a hundred gold bowls. He builds a court for the priests and a great outer court. Huram finishes the pots, shovels, pillars, and stands. The bronze is too much to weigh. The gold altar, tables, lamps, and doors complete the furnishings.
events.detail: Verse 6 separates two uses of water. The ten basins wash the parts of the burnt offerings. The sea is for the priests to wash in. Exodus 30:18–21 required priests to wash before serving. The tabernacle had one lampstand and one table, and the temple has ten. The text describes the objects by the work they do. Regional metalwork offers comparison without reconstructing these exact vessels.

events.title: The ark enters the temple
events.summary: The temple is finished, and Solomon brings in David’s dedicated treasures. The elders gather in Jerusalem at the feast. Levites carry the ark, and the king offers more sacrifices than can be counted. The priests set the ark under the cherubim’s wings. Only the two stone tablets are in it. Singers in fine linen stand with a hundred twenty priests blowing trumpets. They praise the LORD together, for his kindness lasts forever. A cloud fills the house, and the priests cannot stand to serve.
events.detail: Verse 13 stresses unity twice: “as one” and “one sound.” Singers and trumpeters come from different families and duties. Verse 11 says the priests set aside their usual turns for the day. The words they sing are the refrain of Psalm 136. The cloud fills the house at that moment of shared praise. It does not come at the sacrifices in verse 6. Verse 14 says the glory stopped the priests’ work.

events.title: Solomon’s dedication prayer
events.summary: Solomon blesses the people and recalls the promise to David. He kneels on a bronze platform and spreads his hands. He says heaven cannot contain God, much less this house. He asks God to hear prayers made toward this place. He names sin, defeat, drought, famine, and sickness. He prays for the foreigner who comes from far away. He prays for Israel in battle and in exile. He asks God to arise and come to his resting place.
events.detail: Most of the prayer concerns Israel’s own troubles. Verse 32 turns to a person who is “not of your people.” That person has heard of God’s name and power and has traveled far. Verse 33 asks God to do all the foreigner requests. The aim is that all peoples may know and fear God as Israel does. Solomon has already said that God does not live in the house (verse 18). The house serves prayer, including prayer from outside.

events.title: Dedication and a conditional promise
events.summary: When Solomon finishes praying, fire from heaven burns up the offerings. The LORD’s glory fills the house, and the people bow to the ground. The king and people offer thousands of animals. They keep the feast for seven days and the dedication for seven more. The LORD appears to Solomon at night. He promises to hear and heal the land when his people humble themselves and pray. If they turn to other gods, he will uproot them. The house will become a warning to all who pass.
events.detail: Verse 14 is one of the best-known promises in the book. It is half of a speech. Verse 19 begins the other half with “But if.” The “you” in that verse is plural, so it speaks to the nation. Verse 20 says the house itself can be cast away. Verses 21–22 imagine travelers asking why. The promise and the warning are given together on the same night.

events.title: Construction, labor, and sea trade
events.summary: Solomon spends twenty years building the temple and his palace. He rebuilds towns and settles Israelites in them. He fortifies cities for stores, chariots, and horsemen. The remaining Canaanite peoples are made forced laborers. He moves Pharaoh’s daughter out of David’s city. He offers sacrifices on the days and feasts that Moses commanded. He sets the priests, Levites, and gatekeepers in the order David gave. His ships sail with Huram’s sailors and bring gold from Ophir.
events.detail: The building is done, and verse 13 describes what must follow. Offerings are due every day, each Sabbath, each new moon, and at three feasts. The verse says Moses commanded this schedule. Verse 14 adds the priests’ and Levites’ turns that David arranged. Verse 16 then says the house was “completed.” The text counts the work finished when the service is running. A building alone is not the goal.

events.title: Sheba’s queen and Solomon’s reputation
events.summary: The queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon with hard questions. He answers all of them. She sees his house, his table, his servants, and his offerings. She says the report did not tell half of his wisdom. She blesses God, who set him on God’s throne to do justice. She gives gold, spices, and precious stones and returns home. Solomon’s gold, ivory throne, and trading ships are described. He rules forty years and dies.
events.detail: In verse 7 the queen calls Solomon’s servants happy. They hear his wisdom every day. She speaks as a guest who has seen the court at its best. In verse 8 she says God set Solomon on “his throne.” Chronicles thus calls the throne God’s own, where 1 Kings 10:9 says Israel’s. She also names the purpose of a king: justice and righteousness. Chronicles ends Solomon’s story without the failures told in 1 Kings 11.

events.title: Rehoboam refuses relief
events.summary: Rehoboam goes to Shechem, where all Israel has come to make him king. Jeroboam and the people ask him to lighten his father’s heavy yoke. He asks for three days. The old men who served Solomon advise kindness. He rejects their advice and asks the young men he grew up with. They tell him to promise a heavier yoke. He answers the people harshly. Israel rejects David’s house, and only Judah’s towns stay with him.
events.detail: The elders in verse 7 had served Solomon and seen his rule up close. Their advice has three parts: be kind, please the people, speak good words. The result they promise is lasting loyalty. Verse 8 says Rehoboam rejected this before he heard the other advice. He then asks men of his own age. Their answer treats power as something shown by force (verses 10–11). Verse 15 says God was also at work in the outcome.

events.title: Defense, migration, and royal families
events.summary: Rehoboam gathers one hundred eighty thousand soldiers to win back Israel. The prophet Shemaiah brings the LORD’s word against the war. The army listens and goes home. Rehoboam fortifies fifteen cities in Judah and Benjamin. Priests and Levites leave their lands in the north and come to Jerusalem. Jeroboam had removed them and made his own priests. Others who seek the LORD follow them. For three years they strengthen Rehoboam, and his family grows large.
events.detail: Rehoboam has an army ready to restore his kingdom. Verse 4 stops it with one message from one prophet. The message calls the northern tribes “your brothers.” It also says, “this thing is of me.” The division is not to be undone by war. The king and the army obey. Verse 17 reports three good years that follow.

events.title: Shishak and a reduced kingdom
events.summary: When Rehoboam’s rule is strong, he and all Israel abandon the LORD’s law. In his fifth year Shishak king of Egypt attacks Jerusalem. Shemaiah says they left the LORD, so he has left them to Shishak. The king and the leaders humble themselves and say the LORD is right. The LORD grants some rescue and does not destroy them. Shishak takes the treasures of the temple and palace. Rehoboam replaces Solomon’s gold shields with bronze. He rules seventeen years in all.
events.detail: The leaders humble themselves in verse 6, and the LORD relents in verse 7. The rescue is partial. Verse 8 says Judah will still serve Shishak. It also gives the reason: they must learn a difference. Serving God is one thing, and serving foreign kingdoms is another. Verses 9–11 show the cost in gold. Bronze shields then keep up the royal show with cheaper metal.

events.title: Abijah’s speech and war
events.summary: Abijah king of Judah goes to war against Jeroboam. Judah’s army is half the size of Israel’s. Abijah stands on a hill and speaks to the northern army. He says God gave the kingdom to David’s sons. He says the north has golden calves and has driven out the LORD’s priests. Jeroboam sets an ambush behind Judah. Judah cries to the LORD, and the priests blow the trumpets. God defeats Israel, and Abijah takes Bethel and other towns.
events.detail: Abijah’s speech does not boast of soldiers, since he has fewer. His case rests on worship. Judah has Aaron’s priests, daily offerings, and the lamps (verses 10–11). Verse 12 says God is at Judah’s head, with priests and trumpets. He still calls the enemy “children of Israel.” He calls the LORD the God of their fathers too. Verse 18 gives the writer’s reason for the victory: Judah relied on the LORD.

events.title: Asa changes worship and asks for help
events.summary: Asa does what is good and right. He removes foreign altars and tells Judah to seek the LORD. The land has ten years of peace. He builds walled cities and trains a large army. Zerah the Cushite comes against him with a far greater force. Asa prays that the LORD helps the weak as easily as the strong. The LORD strikes the Cushites, and they flee. Judah carries home much plunder, with sheep and camels.
events.detail: Asa has walls, towers, and a trained army (verses 6–8). His prayer in verse 11 does not mention them. He says only the LORD can help, whether the side is strong or weak. He says, “we rely on you.” He also makes the battle God’s: no man should prevail against him. The chapter shows preparation and prayer side by side. Chapter 16 will test whether Asa keeps relying this way.

events.title: Azariah’s warning and covenant
events.summary: God’s Spirit comes on Azariah, who meets Asa after the victory. He says the LORD is with them while they are with him. Israel once lived long without a teaching priest or law. Asa takes courage and removes idols from the land. He repairs the LORD’s altar. Many come to him from the northern tribes. The people swear a covenant with shouting and trumpets and great joy. Asa even removes his grandmother from her position for her idol.
events.detail: Verse 8 says Asa “took courage” when he heard the prophet. Reform takes courage because it reaches into his own house. Verse 16 shows it: he removes his grandmother from her rank. Verse 9 says people from the north joined him. They came when they saw that God was with him. Verse 2 states the rule beneath the whole chapter. The LORD is found by those who seek him.

events.title: Asa’s alliance and anger
events.summary: Baasha king of Israel fortifies Ramah to shut Judah in. Asa sends temple and palace treasure to the king of Syria. Syria attacks Israel’s northern towns, and Baasha stops building. The seer Hanani tells Asa he relied on Syria and not on the LORD. He reminds him of the victory over the Cushites. From now on Asa will have wars. Asa puts the seer in prison and mistreats some of the people. Late in life his feet are diseased, and he seeks only physicians.
events.detail: In 14:11 Asa prayed, “we rely on you.” Hanani uses that same word against him in verses 7–8. The seer’s argument is Asa’s own past. God handled a much larger army when Asa asked. In 15:8 Asa heard a prophet and took courage. In verse 10 he hears one and reaches for the prison. The verse adds that he oppressed some of the people at that time.

events.title: Jehoshaphat teaches and strengthens Judah
events.summary: Jehoshaphat becomes king and strengthens Judah against Israel. He follows the ways of David and does not seek the Baals. The LORD establishes his kingdom, and he grows rich. In his third year he sends officials, Levites, and priests through Judah. They carry the book of the LORD’s law and teach in every city. Fear of the LORD falls on the nearby kingdoms. Philistines and Arabs bring him tribute. He builds forts and keeps a large army.
events.detail: Verses 7–8 name the teaching team. It has five officials, nine Levites, and two priests. Verse 9 says they carried the book of the law with them. They went to the people’s towns; the people did not come to them. Royal officers and temple staff taught together. Verse 10 follows with peace on Judah’s borders. The writer sets that peace beside the teaching before he lists the army.

events.title: Micaiah and the war with Ahab
events.summary: Jehoshaphat is rich and allied to Ahab by marriage. Ahab asks him to help retake Ramoth Gilead. Four hundred prophets promise victory. Jehoshaphat asks for another, and Micaiah is called. Micaiah sees Israel scattered and describes a lying spirit in the prophets’ mouths. Ahab jails him and goes to battle in disguise. The enemy surrounds Jehoshaphat, and he cries out and is spared. A random arrow strikes Ahab, and he dies at sunset.
events.detail: The messenger in verse 12 asks Micaiah to match the others. Four hundred voices already agree, and the kings are waiting. Micaiah answers that he will say what God says (verse 13). Jehoshaphat is the one who asked for a true word (verses 4 and 6). He hears it and still rides into battle (verse 28). Verse 31 says the LORD helped him when he cried out. Chapter 19:2 rebukes him for the alliance.

events.title: Correction and impartial judgment
events.summary: Jehoshaphat returns safely, and the seer Jehu rebukes him for helping the wicked. Yet some good is found in him. The king travels among the people and brings them back to the LORD. He appoints judges in every fortified city. He tells them they judge for the LORD, not for man. In Jerusalem he sets up a court of Levites, priests, and family heads. The chief priest leads in the LORD’s matters. A leader of Judah handles the king’s matters.
events.detail: Jehoshaphat accepts a seer’s rebuke in verses 2–3. His father had jailed that seer’s father (16:10). His response is to reform the courts. Verse 6 tells the judges whose work they do. Verse 7 sets their standard by God’s character. With him there is no injustice, no favoritism, and no bribe. Verse 11 divides religious cases from royal ones under two chiefs.

events.title: Prayer, Jahaziel, and deliverance
events.summary: A great army from Moab, Ammon, and Mount Seir comes against Judah. Jehoshaphat is afraid and calls a fast. All Judah gathers with wives and children. The king prays and admits they have no strength and no plan. The Spirit comes on Jahaziel, a Levite, who says the battle is God’s. Next morning singers march ahead of the army giving thanks. The enemy armies turn on one another. Judah gathers plunder for three days and blesses the LORD.
events.detail: A king is expected to have a plan. In verse 12 Jehoshaphat says in public that he has none. He says, “We don’t know what to do.” Verse 13 notes who is listening: whole families with little ones. The answer comes through a Levite of a singers’ family (verse 14). He says they will not need to fight (verse 17). In verse 21 the king puts a choir ahead of the soldiers.

events.title: Jehoram’s violence and decline
events.summary: Jehoshaphat gives his sons gifts and cities and leaves the kingdom to Jehoram. Jehoram kills all his brothers and some of the princes. He marries Ahab’s daughter and follows Israel’s kings. The LORD spares David’s house because of the covenant. Edom and Libnah revolt. A letter from Elijah says Jehoram will die of disease. Raiders carry off his goods, wives, and sons. He dies in great pain, and no one regrets his death.
events.detail: Verse 3 says the father provided for every son. Jehoram sees his brothers as rivals and kills them (verse 4). The rest of the chapter returns the loss to him. Subject peoples break away (verses 8–10). Raiders take his own sons, all but the youngest (verse 17). Elijah’s letter calls the murdered brothers better men than he (verse 13). Verse 20 says he departed “with no one’s regret.”

events.title: Ahaziah dies and Joash is hidden
events.summary: Ahaziah becomes king of Judah. His mother Athaliah advises him to do evil. He joins Israel’s king in war and visits him at Jezreel. Jehu, who is destroying Ahab’s house, kills Ahaziah too. Athaliah then kills the royal children of Judah. Jehoshabeath, the king’s daughter, steals away the baby Joash. She hides him and his nurse in a bedroom. He stays hidden in God’s house for six years while Athaliah rules.
events.detail: Two women shape this chapter. Verse 3 says Athaliah counseled her son to do wrong. Verse 10 says she killed her own grandchildren for the throne. Verse 11 names the woman who stopped her. Jehoshabeath was a king’s daughter and the wife of the priest Jehoiada. That marriage explains how a child could be hidden in the temple. For six years the line of David depends on her secret.

events.title: Jehoiada installs Joash
events.summary: In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada makes a pact with the guard captains. They gather Levites and family heads from all Judah. Guards surround the young king with weapons from the temple. They crown Joash, hand him the testimony, and shout. Athaliah cries treason and is put to death outside the temple. Jehoiada makes a covenant with the people and the king. They tear down Baal’s temple. Gatekeepers are posted, and the city is quiet.
events.detail: The crowning in verse 11 includes “the testimony.” Deuteronomy 17:18–19 required a king to keep a copy of the law. Verse 16 then binds three parties: priest, people, and king. Its aim is that they should be the LORD’s people. A seven-year-old king is one party among others. The covenant puts duties on the throne, not only a boy. Verses 18–19 restore the temple order that David set.

events.title: Temple repair and Zechariah’s death
events.summary: Joash does right all the days of the priest Jehoiada. He collects money in a chest and repairs the temple. Jehoiada dies very old and is buried among the kings. Then Judah’s princes persuade the king to leave the LORD’s house. Prophets warn them, and they do not listen. The Spirit comes on Zechariah, Jehoiada’s son, who rebukes the people. At the king’s command they stone him in the temple court. A small Syrian army defeats Judah, and Joash’s servants kill him.
events.detail: Jehoiada and his wife saved Joash’s life as a baby (22:11). They hid him in the temple for six years. Verse 22 says the king did not remember that kindness. He has their son killed in the court of that same house (verse 21). Zechariah’s last words ask the LORD to see and repay. The burials tell the verdict. The priest lies among the kings (verse 16), and the king does not (verse 25).

events.title: Amaziah’s victories and defeat
events.summary: Amaziah does right, but not with a whole heart. He hires a hundred thousand soldiers from Israel. A man of God says to send them home, and he obeys at a loss. He defeats Edom and then worships Edom’s gods. A prophet asks why he seeks gods that could not save their own people. The king threatens him into silence. Amaziah challenges Israel’s king and is badly beaten. Jerusalem’s wall is broken, and he later dies by conspiracy.
events.detail: The first warning cost Amaziah a hundred talents of silver (verses 6–9). He asked about the money and still obeyed (verse 10). The second warning comes after a victory. The prophet’s logic in verse 15 is simple: these gods lost. In verse 16 the king cuts him off and hints at violence. He says no one appointed the prophet as a royal adviser. Success has changed how he hears correction.

events.title: Uzziah’s strength and forbidden incense
events.summary: Uzziah becomes king at sixteen and rules fifty-two years. He seeks God, and God gives him success. He defeats the Philistines, builds towers, digs cisterns, and loves farming. His army is large and has new war machines. When he is strong, his heart grows proud. He enters the temple to burn incense on the altar. Eighty priests confront him, and he becomes angry. A skin disease breaks out on his forehead, and he lives apart until he dies.
events.detail: Verse 16 dates the fall: “when he was strong.” Uzziah has succeeded at war, building, and farming. He now reaches for a task that is not a king’s. Numbers 18:7 gives the incense altar to Aaron’s sons alone. In verse 18 eighty-one priests tell the king to leave. Verse 17 calls them men of courage. Verse 19 says the disease appeared while he was raging at them.

events.title: Jotham builds and governs
events.summary: Jotham becomes king at twenty-five and rules sixteen years. He does what is right, as his father Uzziah did. Unlike his father he does not enter the LORD’s temple. The people still act corruptly. He builds the upper gate of the temple and much on the city wall. He builds towns in the hills and forts in the forests. He defeats Ammon, which pays him tribute. He grows strong because he orders his ways before the LORD.
events.detail: Verse 2 makes three statements in a row. Jotham did right. He stayed out of the temple, so he learned from his father’s fall. The people still acted corruptly. A good king, the verse admits, does not make a good people. Verse 6 credits his strength to his own steady conduct. Isaiah 1:1 and Micah 1:1 place those prophets’ warnings in his reign.

events.title: Ahaz, captives, and Oded’s intervention
events.summary: Ahaz makes idols and burns his children as offerings. Syria defeats him and takes captives. Israel’s king kills many of Judah’s soldiers and carries off women and children. The prophet Oded meets the army at Samaria. He says they have killed in rage and must not enslave their kin. Four leaders of Ephraim agree and stop the army. They clothe, feed, and carry the captives back to Jericho. Ahaz then seeks Assyria’s help, worships Syria’s gods, and shuts the temple.
events.detail: Oded does not deny that the victory came from God (verse 9). He denies that it permits enslaving “your brothers.” Verse 10 asks whether the victors have no sins of their own. Verse 11 then gives the order: send them back. Four named leaders face down the army (verses 12–13). Verse 15 lists their care: clothes, sandals, food, oil, and donkeys for the weak. Jesus’s story in Luke 10:33–35 uses several of the same details.

events.title: Hezekiah restores temple service
events.summary: Hezekiah opens the temple doors in the first month of his reign. He tells the priests and Levites to make themselves and the house holy. They carry out the filth and finish in sixteen days. The king and the city leaders bring sin offerings for all Israel. Levites play the instruments David appointed, and the assembly bows. The people bring so many offerings that the priests need help. The Levites assist them. Hezekiah and the people rejoice at how quickly it was done.
events.detail: The chapter follows a set order. First the house is cleaned (verses 15–17). Then offerings are made for sin (verses 21–24). Then the music begins (verses 25–30), and the people bring their gifts (verse 31). Verse 34 admits a shortage of ready priests, and Levites fill the gap. Verse 36 gives the reason for the joy. God had prepared the people, and the work was done “suddenly.”

events.title: Passover invitations and pardon
events.summary: Hezekiah invites all Israel and Judah to keep the Passover in Jerusalem. It is held in the second month because the priests were not ready. Couriers carry letters north to Ephraim and Manasseh. Many laugh at them, but some humble themselves and come. Many who come have not made themselves clean. They eat anyway, and Hezekiah prays for their pardon. The LORD hears him and heals the people. The feast is so glad that they keep it seven more days.
events.detail: Verse 18 admits that the rule was broken. Many from the north ate the Passover without being clean. Hezekiah does not send them away. His prayer asks pardon for all who truly seek God (verses 18–19). Verse 20 says the LORD listened. Even the month was moved to make the feast possible (verses 2–3). Numbers 9:10–11 had allowed a second-month Passover for people who were not ready.

events.title: Offerings and faithful distribution
events.summary: After the feast the people break down the idols and altars across the land. Hezekiah sets the priests and Levites in their turns of service. He gives from his own herds for the regular offerings. He tells the people to give the priests’ and Levites’ share. They bring grain, wine, oil, and honey in heaps for four months. The chief priest says there is enough and plenty left over. Storerooms are prepared and keepers named. Men are chosen to hand out portions fairly in every town.
events.detail: Verse 4 gives the purpose of the gifts. Priests and Levites should be free to give themselves to the LORD’s law. The people respond with heaps (verses 5–7). Verse 10 reports enough to eat and much to spare. Verses 12–15 name the keepers and require fair shares for great and small. Verse 18 extends the list to wives, sons, daughters, and little ones. Worship continues because whole households are fed.

events.title: Sennacherib’s challenge and Hezekiah’s response
events.summary: Sennacherib of Assyria invades Judah and camps against its walled cities. Hezekiah stops the springs outside Jerusalem and repairs the wall. He makes weapons and tells the people that a greater one is with them. Assyrian officers shout insults at the people on the wall. Hezekiah and Isaiah cry to heaven. An angel destroys the Assyrian commanders, and Sennacherib goes home in shame. Later Hezekiah is sick, grows proud, and humbles himself. He also brings water down to the west side of David’s city.
events.detail: Hezekiah’s first response is practical. He blocks the water an army would need (verses 3–4). Verse 5 lists a repaired wall, towers, a second wall, and weapons. His speech in verses 7–8 then asks the people to trust God. The account sets defense and prayer together. Assyrian records describe the campaign from the attacking king’s side. Chronicles leaves out the tribute reported in 2 Kings 18:14–16.

events.title: Manasseh’s repentance and Amon’s refusal
events.summary: Manasseh rules fifty-five years and does great evil. He rebuilds the high places and sets an idol in God’s house. He burns his sons, uses sorcery, and ignores every warning. Assyrian commanders capture him and take him to Babylon in chains. In distress he humbles himself and prays. God hears and brings him back to Jerusalem. He removes the idols and repairs the LORD’s altar. His son Amon does evil, does not humble himself, and is killed.
events.detail: Second Kings 21 tells of Manasseh’s sins and nothing more. Chronicles adds a capture, a prayer, and a return (verses 11–13). Verse 12 marks the turn: he was in distress, and he humbled himself. Verse 13 says God was moved and heard him. The worst king in the book is not beyond being heard. His reform is real but incomplete (verse 17). Verse 23 says Amon did not humble himself as his father had.

events.title: Josiah changes worship and seeks Huldah's answer
events.summary: Josiah becomes king at eight. At sixteen he begins to seek God, and at twenty he clears away the idols. He carries the reform into the northern lands. In his eighteenth year he repairs the temple with honest workmen. While the money is brought out, the priest Hilkiah finds the book of the law. The king hears it and tears his clothes. His officials consult the prophetess Huldah, who confirms the coming disaster. Josiah gathers the people and renews the covenant.
events.detail: In Chronicles Josiah has been reforming for years before the book appears (verses 3–7). The book is found during ordinary work with the temple money (verse 14). Its words still make him tear his clothes (verse 19). A sincere reformer learns how much he did not know. Verse 22 sends his chief officials to Huldah. She speaks for the LORD and confirms what the book says (verses 23–25). Her answer leads to a public covenant (verses 29–32).

events.title: Josiah’s Passover and death
events.summary: Josiah keeps the Passover in Jerusalem on the proper day. He sets the priests and Levites in their places. He and his officials give thousands of animals for the people. No Passover like it had been kept since Samuel’s time. Later Pharaoh Neco marches north to fight at Carchemish. Josiah goes out against him. Neco says God sent him and warns Josiah to turn back. Josiah fights in disguise, is shot by archers, and dies in Jerusalem.
events.detail: Verse 20 begins “After all this,” meaning after the temple and the Passover. Josiah’s record gives no protection for the next choice. The warning comes from a foreign king (verse 21). Verse 22 says his words were “from the mouth of God.” Josiah once sent to a prophetess to test a book. Here he does not ask anyone. His disguise recalls Ahab’s in 18:29, and it works no better.

events.title: Exile and Cyrus’s proclamation
events.summary: Judah’s last four kings rule under Egypt and then Babylon. Zedekiah will not humble himself before the prophet Jeremiah. He breaks an oath he swore by God to Nebuchadnezzar. The LORD sends messengers again and again, out of pity for his people. They mock the prophets until there is no remedy. The Babylonians kill, burn the temple, and break down Jerusalem’s wall. The survivors become servants in Babylon for seventy years. Then Cyrus king of Persia permits the people to go up and rebuild.
events.detail: Verses 15–16 explain the exile before verse 23 ends it. God sent messengers out of compassion, and they were mocked. The final speech comes from Cyrus, a foreign ruler. It allows a return and the rebuilding of a temple. The book’s last words are “let him go up.” The Cyrus Cylinder gives wider context for Persian restoration claims. It does not name this return or prove every detail of the speech.
