ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Lachish–Jerusalem approaches
ancientRoads.summary: Routes through the Shephelah valleys connected Lachish with Jerusalem. They also joined nearby walled towns with the Judean hills.
ancientRoads.detail: Second Kings 18:17 sends an Assyrian army from Lachish up to Jerusalem. The text does not name the road. This line shows one common approach.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact track is unknown, so the line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Aleppo–Euphrates approach
ancientRoads.summary: This road linked Aleppo with the Euphrates crossing near Til Barsip. Assyria’s state road began there.
ancientRoads.detail: Assyrian records and studies of ancient land support this route. It went through the Sajur and Manbij area. It then crossed the Jabbul plain toward Aleppo.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection and principal approach are well supported. The displayed bends simplify several local valleys and possible parallel tracks.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian King’s Road to Nineveh
ancientRoads.summary: The Neo-Assyrian state road connected western lands with the Assyrian heartland. It ended at the capital city of Nineveh.
ancientRoads.detail: The route crossed the Euphrates at Til Barsip. It crossed the Balih south of Harran. It also crossed Habur streams between Guzana and Nasibina. It then reached the Tigris at Nineveh. Royal messengers changed mules at road stations.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The named crossings and stations are well supported. The line between them is a broad regional path, not a surveyed roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian Tigris route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route followed the Tigris. It linked Nineveh, Kalhu, and Assur in the Assyrian heartland.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu held a central position between Assur and Nineveh. It supported long trips by land and river. Kalhu later became an Assyrian royal capital.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The cities and their connection are well supported. The line shows a broad route. It does not separate land travel from river travel at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Arbela–Babylonia route
ancientRoads.summary: An eastern branch connected Kalhu with Arbela. It followed the western edge of the Zagros Mountains. Other routes continued south into Babylonia.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu controlled an eastward route through Arbela. The route followed the western edge of the Zagros toward Babylonia. It avoided a direct crossing of the central desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is supported, but the precise southern alignment and stations are uncertain. The line is dashed.

guides.title: 2 Chronicles: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Water and metal serve different tasks
steps.text: Verse 6 separates two uses of water. The ten basins wash the parts of the burnt offerings. The sea is for the priests to wash in. Exodus 30:18–21 required priests to wash before serving. The tabernacle had one lampstand and one table, and the temple has ten. The text describes the objects by the work they do. Regional metalwork offers comparison without reconstructing these exact vessels.

steps.title: Defense combines work and trust
steps.text: Hezekiah’s first response is practical. He blocks the water an army would need (verses 3–4). Verse 5 lists a repaired wall, towers, a second wall, and weapons. His speech in verses 7–8 then asks the people to trust God. The account sets defense and prayer together. Assyrian records describe the campaign from the attacking king’s side. Chronicles leaves out the tribute reported in 2 Kings 18:14–16.

steps.title: The last royal speech opens a road beyond exile
steps.text: Verses 15–16 explain the exile before verse 23 ends it. God sent messengers out of compassion, and they were mocked. The final speech comes from Cyrus, a foreign ruler. It allows a return and the rebuilding of a temple. The book’s last words are “let him go up.” The Cyrus Cylinder gives wider context for Persian restoration claims. It does not name this return or prove every detail of the speech.

chapterMaps.narrative: Solomon is established as king, and God is with him. He leads the assembly to Gibeon, where the tent of meeting stands. He offers a thousand burnt offerings on the bronze altar. That night God tells him to ask for whatever he wants. Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge to lead the people. God gives him that, with riches and honor besides. Solomon gathers chariots and horsemen. He buys horses from Egypt and makes silver common in Jerusalem.

chapterMaps.narrative: Solomon decides to build a house for the LORD’s name and a palace. He writes to Huram king of Tyre for cedar and a master craftsman. He admits that even the highest heaven cannot contain God. He offers wheat, barley, wine, and oil for Tyre’s woodcutters. Huram praises the LORD and sends a craftsman of mixed descent. The logs will come by sea to Joppa. Solomon counts the foreigners living in Israel. He makes them carriers, stonecutters, and overseers.

chapterMaps.narrative: Solomon begins to build the LORD’s house in Jerusalem. The site is Mount Moriah, at the threshing floor of Ornan. He starts in the fourth year of his reign. The main room is overlaid with fine gold and set with precious stones. The inner room holds two great cherubim whose wings span the width. A veil of blue, purple, and crimson hangs before it. Two tall pillars stand in front of the house. They are named Jachin and Boaz.

chapterMaps.narrative: Solomon makes a bronze altar twenty cubits square. He makes the great basin called the sea, resting on twelve oxen. He makes ten smaller basins and ten gold lampstands. He makes ten tables and a hundred gold bowls. He builds a court for the priests and a great outer court. Huram finishes the pots, shovels, pillars, and stands. The bronze is too much to weigh. The gold altar, tables, lamps, and doors complete the furnishings.

chapterMaps.narrative: The temple is finished, and Solomon brings in David’s dedicated treasures. The elders gather in Jerusalem at the feast. Levites carry the ark, and the king offers more sacrifices than can be counted. The priests set the ark under the cherubim’s wings. Only the two stone tablets are in it. Singers in fine linen stand with a hundred twenty priests blowing trumpets. They praise the LORD together, for his kindness lasts forever. A cloud fills the house, and the priests cannot stand to serve.

chapterMaps.narrative: Solomon blesses the people and recalls the promise to David. He kneels on a bronze platform and spreads his hands. He says heaven cannot contain God, much less this house. He asks God to hear prayers made toward this place. He names sin, defeat, drought, famine, and sickness. He prays for the foreigner who comes from far away. He prays for Israel in battle and in exile. He asks God to arise and come to his resting place.

chapterMaps.narrative: When Solomon finishes praying, fire from heaven burns up the offerings. The LORD’s glory fills the house, and the people bow to the ground. The king and people offer thousands of animals. They keep the feast for seven days and the dedication for seven more. The LORD appears to Solomon at night. He promises to hear and heal the land when his people humble themselves and pray. If they turn to other gods, he will uproot them. The house will become a warning to all who pass.

chapterMaps.narrative: Solomon spends twenty years building the temple and his palace. He rebuilds towns and settles Israelites in them. He fortifies cities for stores, chariots, and horsemen. The remaining Canaanite peoples are made forced laborers. He moves Pharaoh’s daughter out of David’s city. He offers sacrifices on the days and feasts that Moses commanded. He sets the priests, Levites, and gatekeepers in the order David gave. His ships sail with Huram’s sailors and bring gold from Ophir.

chapterMaps.narrative: The queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon with hard questions. He answers all of them. She sees his house, his table, his servants, and his offerings. She says the report did not tell half of his wisdom. She blesses God, who set him on God’s throne to do justice. She gives gold, spices, and precious stones and returns home. Solomon’s gold, ivory throne, and trading ships are described. He rules forty years and dies.

chapterMaps.narrative: Rehoboam goes to Shechem, where all Israel has come to make him king. Jeroboam and the people ask him to lighten his father’s heavy yoke. He asks for three days. The old men who served Solomon advise kindness. He rejects their advice and asks the young men he grew up with. They tell him to promise a heavier yoke. He answers the people harshly. Israel rejects David’s house, and only Judah’s towns stay with him.

chapterMaps.narrative: Rehoboam gathers one hundred eighty thousand soldiers to win back Israel. The prophet Shemaiah brings the LORD’s word against the war. The army listens and goes home. Rehoboam fortifies fifteen cities in Judah and Benjamin. Priests and Levites leave their lands in the north and come to Jerusalem. Jeroboam had removed them and made his own priests. Others who seek the LORD follow them. For three years they strengthen Rehoboam, and his family grows large.

chapterMaps.narrative: When Rehoboam’s rule is strong, he and all Israel abandon the LORD’s law. In his fifth year Shishak king of Egypt attacks Jerusalem. Shemaiah says they left the LORD, so he has left them to Shishak. The king and the leaders humble themselves and say the LORD is right. The LORD grants some rescue and does not destroy them. Shishak takes the treasures of the temple and palace. Rehoboam replaces Solomon’s gold shields with bronze. He rules seventeen years in all.

chapterMaps.narrative: Abijah king of Judah goes to war against Jeroboam. Judah’s army is half the size of Israel’s. Abijah stands on a hill and speaks to the northern army. He says God gave the kingdom to David’s sons. He says the north has golden calves and has driven out the LORD’s priests. Jeroboam sets an ambush behind Judah. Judah cries to the LORD, and the priests blow the trumpets. God defeats Israel, and Abijah takes Bethel and other towns.

chapterMaps.narrative: Asa does what is good and right. He removes foreign altars and tells Judah to seek the LORD. The land has ten years of peace. He builds walled cities and trains a large army. Zerah the Cushite comes against him with a far greater force. Asa prays that the LORD helps the weak as easily as the strong. The LORD strikes the Cushites, and they flee. Judah carries home much plunder, with sheep and camels.

chapterMaps.note: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.
chapterMaps.narrative: God’s Spirit comes on Azariah, who meets Asa after the victory. He says the LORD is with them while they are with him. Israel once lived long without a teaching priest or law. Asa takes courage and removes idols from the land. He repairs the LORD’s altar. Many come to him from the northern tribes. The people swear a covenant with shouting and trumpets and great joy. Asa even removes his grandmother from her position for her idol.

chapterMaps.narrative: Baasha king of Israel fortifies Ramah to shut Judah in. Asa sends temple and palace treasure to the king of Syria. Syria attacks Israel’s northern towns, and Baasha stops building. The seer Hanani tells Asa he relied on Syria and not on the LORD. He reminds him of the victory over the Cushites. From now on Asa will have wars. Asa puts the seer in prison and mistreats some of the people. Late in life his feet are diseased, and he seeks only physicians.

chapterMaps.narrative: Jehoshaphat becomes king and strengthens Judah against Israel. He follows the ways of David and does not seek the Baals. The LORD establishes his kingdom, and he grows rich. In his third year he sends officials, Levites, and priests through Judah. They carry the book of the LORD’s law and teach in every city. Fear of the LORD falls on the nearby kingdoms. Philistines and Arabs bring him tribute. He builds forts and keeps a large army.
chapterMaps.limits: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.

chapterMaps.narrative: Jehoshaphat is rich and allied to Ahab by marriage. Ahab asks him to help retake Ramoth Gilead. Four hundred prophets promise victory. Jehoshaphat asks for another, and Micaiah is called. Micaiah sees Israel scattered and describes a lying spirit in the prophets’ mouths. Ahab jails him and goes to battle in disguise. The enemy surrounds Jehoshaphat, and he cries out and is spared. A random arrow strikes Ahab, and he dies at sunset.

chapterMaps.note: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.
chapterMaps.narrative: Jehoshaphat returns safely, and the seer Jehu rebukes him for helping the wicked. Yet some good is found in him. The king travels among the people and brings them back to the LORD. He appoints judges in every fortified city. He tells them they judge for the LORD, not for man. In Jerusalem he sets up a court of Levites, priests, and family heads. The chief priest leads in the LORD’s matters. A leader of Judah handles the king’s matters.

chapterMaps.narrative: A great army from Moab, Ammon, and Mount Seir comes against Judah. Jehoshaphat is afraid and calls a fast. All Judah gathers with wives and children. The king prays and admits they have no strength and no plan. The Spirit comes on Jahaziel, a Levite, who says the battle is God’s. Next morning singers march ahead of the army giving thanks. The enemy armies turn on one another. Judah gathers plunder for three days and blesses the LORD.
chapterMaps.limits: Lines join the places 2 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

chapterMaps.note: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.
chapterMaps.narrative: Jehoshaphat gives his sons gifts and cities and leaves the kingdom to Jehoram. Jehoram kills all his brothers and some of the princes. He marries Ahab’s daughter and follows Israel’s kings. The LORD spares David’s house because of the covenant. Edom and Libnah revolt. A letter from Elijah says Jehoram will die of disease. Raiders carry off his goods, wives, and sons. He dies in great pain, and no one regrets his death.

chapterMaps.narrative: Ahaziah becomes king of Judah. His mother Athaliah advises him to do evil. He joins Israel’s king in war and visits him at Jezreel. Jehu, who is destroying Ahab’s house, kills Ahaziah too. Athaliah then kills the royal children of Judah. Jehoshabeath, the king’s daughter, steals away the baby Joash. She hides him and his nurse in a bedroom. He stays hidden in God’s house for six years while Athaliah rules.

chapterMaps.narrative: In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada makes a pact with the guard captains. They gather Levites and family heads from all Judah. Guards surround the young king with weapons from the temple. They crown Joash, hand him the testimony, and shout. Athaliah cries treason and is put to death outside the temple. Jehoiada makes a covenant with the people and the king. They tear down Baal’s temple. Gatekeepers are posted, and the city is quiet.

chapterMaps.note: Points mark named towns and broad regions in the book. Many ancient sites are only roughly placed.
chapterMaps.narrative: Joash does right all the days of the priest Jehoiada. He collects money in a chest and repairs the temple. Jehoiada dies very old and is buried among the kings. Then Judah’s princes persuade the king to leave the LORD’s house. Prophets warn them, and they do not listen. The Spirit comes on Zechariah, Jehoiada’s son, who rebukes the people. At the king’s command they stone him in the temple court. A small Syrian army defeats Judah, and Joash’s servants kill him.

chapterMaps.narrative: Amaziah does right, but not with a whole heart. He hires a hundred thousand soldiers from Israel. A man of God says to send them home, and he obeys at a loss. He defeats Edom and then worships Edom’s gods. A prophet asks why he seeks gods that could not save their own people. The king threatens him into silence. Amaziah challenges Israel’s king and is badly beaten. Jerusalem’s wall is broken, and he later dies by conspiracy.

chapterMaps.narrative: Uzziah becomes king at sixteen and rules fifty-two years. He seeks God, and God gives him success. He defeats the Philistines, builds towers, digs cisterns, and loves farming. His army is large and has new war machines. When he is strong, his heart grows proud. He enters the temple to burn incense on the altar. Eighty priests confront him, and he becomes angry. A skin disease breaks out on his forehead, and he lives apart until he dies.

chapterMaps.narrative: Jotham becomes king at twenty-five and rules sixteen years. He does what is right, as his father Uzziah did. Unlike his father he does not enter the LORD’s temple. The people still act corruptly. He builds the upper gate of the temple and much on the city wall. He builds towns in the hills and forts in the forests. He defeats Ammon, which pays him tribute. He grows strong because he orders his ways before the LORD.

chapterMaps.narrative: Ahaz makes idols and burns his children as offerings. Syria defeats him and takes captives. Israel’s king kills many of Judah’s soldiers and carries off women and children. The prophet Oded meets the army at Samaria. He says they have killed in rage and must not enslave their kin. Four leaders of Ephraim agree and stop the army. They clothe, feed, and carry the captives back to Jericho. Ahaz then seeks Assyria’s help, worships Syria’s gods, and shuts the temple.

chapterMaps.narrative: Hezekiah opens the temple doors in the first month of his reign. He tells the priests and Levites to make themselves and the house holy. They carry out the filth and finish in sixteen days. The king and the city leaders bring sin offerings for all Israel. Levites play the instruments David appointed, and the assembly bows. The people bring so many offerings that the priests need help. The Levites assist them. Hezekiah and the people rejoice at how quickly it was done.

chapterMaps.narrative: Hezekiah invites all Israel and Judah to keep the Passover in Jerusalem. It is held in the second month because the priests were not ready. Couriers carry letters north to Ephraim and Manasseh. Many laugh at them, but some humble themselves and come. Many who come have not made themselves clean. They eat anyway, and Hezekiah prays for their pardon. The LORD hears him and heals the people. The feast is so glad that they keep it seven more days.

chapterMaps.narrative: After the feast the people break down the idols and altars across the land. Hezekiah sets the priests and Levites in their turns of service. He gives from his own herds for the regular offerings. He tells the people to give the priests’ and Levites’ share. They bring grain, wine, oil, and honey in heaps for four months. The chief priest says there is enough and plenty left over. Storerooms are prepared and keepers named. Men are chosen to hand out portions fairly in every town.

chapterMaps.narrative: Sennacherib of Assyria invades Judah and camps against its walled cities. Hezekiah stops the springs outside Jerusalem and repairs the wall. He makes weapons and tells the people that a greater one is with them. Assyrian officers shout insults at the people on the wall. Hezekiah and Isaiah cry to heaven. An angel destroys the Assyrian commanders, and Sennacherib goes home in shame. Later Hezekiah is sick, grows proud, and humbles himself. He also brings water down to the west side of David’s city.

chapterMaps.narrative: Manasseh rules fifty-five years and does great evil. He rebuilds the high places and sets an idol in God’s house. He burns his sons, uses sorcery, and ignores every warning. Assyrian commanders capture him and take him to Babylon in chains. In distress he humbles himself and prays. God hears and brings him back to Jerusalem. He removes the idols and repairs the LORD’s altar. His son Amon does evil, does not humble himself, and is killed.

chapterMaps.narrative: Josiah becomes king at eight. At sixteen he begins to seek God, and at twenty he clears away the idols. He carries the reform into the northern lands. In his eighteenth year he repairs the temple with honest workmen. While the money is brought out, the priest Hilkiah finds the book of the law. The king hears it and tears his clothes. His officials consult the prophetess Huldah, who confirms the coming disaster. Josiah gathers the people and renews the covenant.

chapterMaps.narrative: Josiah keeps the Passover in Jerusalem on the proper day. He sets the priests and Levites in their places. He and his officials give thousands of animals for the people. No Passover like it had been kept since Samuel’s time. Later Pharaoh Neco marches north to fight at Carchemish. Josiah goes out against him. Neco says God sent him and warns Josiah to turn back. Josiah fights in disguise, is shot by archers, and dies in Jerusalem.

chapterMaps.narrative: Judah’s last four kings rule under Egypt and then Babylon. Zedekiah will not humble himself before the prophet Jeremiah. He breaks an oath he swore by God to Nebuchadnezzar. The LORD sends messengers again and again, out of pity for his people. They mock the prophets until there is no remedy. The Babylonians kill, burn the temple, and break down Jerusalem’s wall. The survivors become servants in Babylon for seventy years. Then Cyrus king of Persia permits the people to go up and rebuild.
